entries.title: Circumcision and Naming of Jesus
entries.blurb: The eighth day of Christmas: the child is circumcised and given the name Jesus — 'the LORD saves' — the name the angel gave before he was conceived.

entries.title: The Topeka outpouring
entries.blurb: At a small Bible school in Topeka, Kansas, a student named Agnes Ozman asks for prayer and begins to speak in an unknown tongue. Charles Parham's students had gone to Acts to ask what the baptism in the Spirit looked like; the answer they believed they found here would be carried to Azusa Street five years later, and from there to the world.

entries.title: Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus
entries.blurb: The two friends among the Cappadocian Fathers, commemorated together. Between them they defended the full deity of the Spirit, gave the Nicene faith its settled language, and left the East a pattern of pastoral care and monastic life it has never abandoned.

entries.title: Luther excommunicated
entries.blurb: The bull Decet Romanum Pontificem formally excommunicates Martin Luther after he refused to recant — cutting the reformer loose from the Roman Church. See the vault's Protestant Reformation note.

entries.title: Epiphany — the Magi (and, in the East, the Baptism of Christ)
entries.blurb: The manifestation of Christ to the Gentiles in the visit of the Magi. Eastern churches keep this day as Theophany, commemorating Jesus' baptism in the Jordan.

entries.title: Five missionaries martyred in Ecuador
entries.blurb: Jim Elliot, Nate Saint, Ed McCully, Peter Fleming and Roger Youderian are speared on a river beach by the Waodani people they had come to reach. Elliot's journal had already answered: 'He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.'

entries.title: Antony of Egypt
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the father of Christian monasticism, who gave away his goods and withdrew to the Egyptian desert; his Life by Athanasius shaped the monastic movement.

entries.title: The Confession of Peter
entries.blurb: Marking Peter's great confession — 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.' The day opens the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

entries.title: The first believers' baptism at Zurich
entries.blurb: In a house near the Zurich fish market, Conrad Grebel baptizes George Blaurock at his own request, and Blaurock baptizes the rest — grown men and women confessing faith and being baptized on it. The city council had forbidden exactly this the day before. The Anabaptist movement, and with it every free church that gathers on believers' baptism, begins in that room.

entries.title: The Conversion of Paul
entries.blurb: The risen Christ confronts Saul on the road to Damascus, turning the church's fiercest persecutor into its greatest missionary. The day closes the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

entries.title: Timothy and Titus
entries.blurb: Feast of the two young co-workers of Paul, entrusted with the churches of Ephesus and Crete, to whom three of his letters are addressed.

entries.title: Presentation of Jesus at the Temple (Candlemas)
entries.blurb: Forty days after the Nativity, Jesus is presented in the Temple, where Simeon greets him as 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles.'

entries.title: Anskar, apostle of the North
entries.blurb: The monk sent from Frankish lands into Denmark and Sweden, who built the first churches of Scandinavia and saw most of his work undone in his lifetime. What he planted took root a century later — a reminder that a missionary's harvest is not always his own to see.

entries.title: The Martyrs of Japan
entries.blurb: Twenty-six Christians — Franciscan missionaries, Jesuits and Japanese laymen, the youngest a boy of twelve — are crucified on a hill above Nagasaki as Japan closes against the faith. The church went underground for two and a half centuries and was found still praying when the country reopened.

entries.title: Cyril and Methodius, apostles to the Slavs
entries.blurb: The brother-missionaries who evangelised the Slavic peoples and devised the alphabet that carried Scripture and liturgy into their tongue.

entries.title: Martin Luther
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the reformer on the day he died at Eisleben, the town where he was born. Lutheran and Anglican calendars keep the day — not for the man's temper or his worst pages, but for the recovery he was given to make: that a sinner is justified by grace through faith, and that the Bible belongs in the people's own tongue. See the vault's Martin Luther note.

entries.title: Polycarp of Smyrna
entries.blurb: Bishop of Smyrna and a hearer of the apostle John, burned in the stadium as an old man. Told to curse Christ and go free, he answered that he had served him eighty-six years and been done no wrong by him. The account of his death is the church's earliest surviving martyrdom story after the New Testament.

entries.title: Matthias the Apostle
entries.blurb: The disciple chosen by lot to take Judas's place among the Twelve — the one apostle the risen Christ did not call in person, and of whom Scripture afterwards says nothing at all. The older Western calendar keeps his day here; Rome now keeps it on 14 May.

entries.title: Edict of Thessalonica
entries.blurb: Emperor Theodosius I makes Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire — a decisive turn from persecuted faith to established church.

entries.title: David of Wales
entries.blurb: Wales's own bishop and patron, remembered for a monastic rule so plain his monks pulled the ploughs themselves. His reported last words to them were to be joyful, keep the faith, and do the little things they had seen him do.

entries.title: Perpetua and Felicity
entries.blurb: A young noblewoman of Carthage and the slave woman imprisoned with her, killed in the arena for refusing to sacrifice to the emperor. Perpetua's prison diary — one of the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman — records her father begging her to recant and her plain refusal to call herself anything but a Christian.

entries.title: Thomas Aquinas
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the Dominican 'Angelic Doctor' on the day of his death, en route to the Council of Lyon — the older Western calendar kept his feast this day. His Summa Theologiae remains the most influential system of theology the medieval church produced.

entries.title: British and Foreign Bible Society founded
entries.blurb: Founded in London to put the Scriptures — 'without note or comment' — into every language and every hand, the Bible Society opens the great century of Bible translation and distribution.

entries.title: Gregory the Great
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the monk-pope who sent Augustine's mission to the English and shaped the worship, pastoral care and chant of the Western church. Kept this day — his death — in the older calendars; the modern Roman feast is 3 September.

entries.title: Patrick, missionary to Ireland
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the fifth-century bishop who, once a captive slave in Ireland, returned to evangelise the island. Traditionally kept on the day of his death.

entries.title: Joseph of Nazareth
entries.blurb: Feast of the carpenter of Nazareth, husband of Mary and guardian of the child Jesus — the 'just man' who obeyed the angel's word.

entries.title: Thomas Cranmer burned at Oxford
entries.blurb: Under Mary's restoration of Rome, the archbishop who gave England the Book of Common Prayer had signed recantations in prison. Brought out to be burned anyway, he took them back in front of the crowd — and in the fire held out first the hand that had signed them. His Prayer Book still shapes how English-speaking Christians pray.

entries.title: Óscar Romero assassinated
entries.blurb: The archbishop of San Salvador is shot at the altar, a day after publicly ordering the country's soldiers to stop killing their own people. A cautious churchman when appointed, he had been changed by burying the poor of his own diocese — and the church he was killed in front of has since named him a martyr.

entries.title: The Annunciation
entries.blurb: Gabriel announces to Mary that she will bear the Son of God — nine months before Christmas. Her answer: 'Let it be to me according to your word.'

entries.title: The Slave Trade Act receives royal assent
entries.blurb: On the feast of the Annunciation, Britain abolishes the transatlantic slave trade — the fruit of the twenty-year parliamentary campaign of William Wilberforce and the Clapham evangelicals.

entries.title: The Assemblies of God constituted
entries.blurb: Around three hundred preachers gather in an old opera house at Hot Springs, Arkansas, to bring order to a revival that had spread faster than anyone could shepherd it — agreeing on doctrine, missions and ministerial credentials without surrendering local church independence. The fellowship they formed is now the largest Pentecostal family in the world.

entries.title: Dennis Bennett tells his parish
entries.blurb: The rector of a comfortable Episcopal church in Van Nuys, California, tells his congregation from the pulpit that he has been baptized in the Spirit and has spoken in tongues. He resigned the same day — and the story went national. What had been a Pentecostal movement outside the historic churches was now loose inside them.

entries.title: The Great Western Schism begins
entries.blurb: The conclave elects Urban VI; within months the French cardinals repudiate him and elect a rival, leaving Western Christendom with two — later three — competing popes for nearly forty years.

entries.title: The Azusa Street Revival begins
entries.blurb: In a Los Angeles mission on Azusa Street, a revival under William Seymour ignites in April 1906 — widely reckoned the birthplace of the worldwide Pentecostal movement.

entries.title: Dietrich Bonhoeffer executed at Flossenbürg
entries.blurb: The theologian of the Confessing Church is hanged for his part in the resistance against Hitler, weeks before the camp's liberation. 'When Christ calls a man,' he had written, 'he bids him come and die.'

entries.title: Luther before the Diet of Worms
entries.blurb: Ordered to recant, Luther refused unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason — the words later summarised as 'Here I stand; I can do no other.' See the vault's Protestant Reformation note.

entries.title: Anselm of Canterbury
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the archbishop and father of scholastic theology — 'faith seeking understanding' — whose Cur Deus Homo reshaped how the West speaks of the atonement.

entries.title: George, martyr
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the soldier-martyr of the Diocletian persecution, later patron of England and of many lands East and West.

entries.title: Adalbert of Prague, martyr
entries.blurb: The missionary bishop of Prague is martyred among the pagan Prussians on the Baltic frontier — an early witness of the gospel's push into northern Europe.

entries.title: Mark the Evangelist
entries.blurb: Feast of the writer of the second Gospel, traditionally the interpreter of Peter and founder of the church in Alexandria.

entries.title: Catherine of Siena
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the Dominican tertiary of Siena, counsellor of popes, who pressed Gregory XI to return the papacy from Avignon to Rome and left a body of letters and the Dialogue.

entries.title: Philip and James, Apostles
entries.blurb: Joint feast of two of the Twelve — Philip, who brought Nathanael to Jesus, and James 'the Less.'

entries.title: The King James Version published
entries.blurb: By the traditional reckoning the 'Authorized Version' is published in London — the translation whose cadences would shape English-speaking faith and language for four centuries. The exact day is uncertain; early May 1611 is the customary date.

entries.title: First Council of Nicaea opens
entries.blurb: The first ecumenical council, convened by Constantine, meets to answer the Arian controversy and gives the church the original Nicene Creed. See the vault's Constantine and Athanasius of Alexandria notes.

entries.title: Wesley's Aldersgate experience
entries.blurb: At a meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, John Wesley felt his heart 'strangely warmed' and trusted Christ alone for salvation — a turning point for the Evangelical Revival.

entries.title: Bede the Venerable
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the monk of Jarrow, 'father of English history,' who died on the eve of Ascension 735 still dictating his English translation of John's Gospel.

entries.title: Augustine of Canterbury
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the reluctant missionary Gregory the Great sent to Kent in 597 — first archbishop of Canterbury, whose mission planted the English church.

entries.title: The Apostolic Faith Mission constituted
entries.blurb: In May 1908 the Pentecostal work John G. Lake and Thomas Hezmalhalch had begun in Doornfontein, Johannesburg gives itself a constitution and an executive — South Africa's first Pentecostal church. It began as a mixed congregation, conformed to segregation under pressure, and only reunited across those lines in 1996.

entries.title: The Fall of Constantinople
entries.blurb: The Byzantine capital falls to the Ottoman Turks, ending the thousand-year Eastern Roman Empire and turning the great church of Hagia Sophia into a mosque — a watershed for Eastern Christianity.

entries.title: The Visitation
entries.blurb: Mary visits Elizabeth, who greets her as 'the mother of my Lord,' and Mary answers with the Magnificat: 'My soul magnifies the Lord.'

entries.title: The Barmen Declaration adopted
entries.blurb: The Confessing Church synod at Barmen adopts its declaration against the Nazi-aligned 'German Christians' — the church belongs to Christ alone and hears no other voice. Drafted chiefly by Karl Barth.

entries.title: Justin Martyr
entries.blurb: A philosopher who kept his cloak after conversion because he believed he had finally found the true philosophy. He wrote the first great defences of the faith to a hostile empire, left the earliest description we have of an ordinary Sunday service, and was beheaded in Rome for refusing to sacrifice.

entries.title: The Uganda Martyrs
entries.blurb: Commemoration of Charles Lwanga and his companions, pages of the Buganda court burned at Namugongo for refusing to renounce Christ — seed of one of Africa's fastest-growing churches.

entries.title: Boniface, apostle to the Germans
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the English monk who evangelised the German lands — felling the pagan Oak of Thor — and was martyred at Dokkum with his companions.

entries.title: Columba of Iona
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the Irish abbot whose island monastery of Iona became the base for the evangelisation of Scotland and the north of England.

entries.title: Barnabas the Apostle
entries.blurb: Feast of the 'son of encouragement,' the Levite who vouched for the converted Paul and travelled with him on the first missionary journey.

entries.title: The Edinburgh Missionary Conference opens
entries.blurb: The World Missionary Conference opens in Edinburgh — some 1,200 delegates surveying the evangelisation of the world in their generation; commonly counted the birthplace of the modern ecumenical movement.

entries.title: Exsurge Domine threatens Luther
entries.blurb: Pope Leo X issues the bull Exsurge Domine, condemning 41 of Luther's propositions and giving him sixty days to recant — the formal opening of Rome's case against the Reformation.

entries.title: Council of Ephesus opens
entries.blurb: The third ecumenical council affirms that Mary bore one who is truly God (Theotokos) and condemns Nestorius — safeguarding the unity of Christ's person.

entries.title: Nativity of John the Baptist
entries.blurb: Kept six months before Christmas, marking the birth of the forerunner who would 'prepare the way of the Lord.'

entries.title: The Augsburg Confession presented
entries.blurb: The foundational Lutheran statement of faith is read before Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg — the confessional charter of the Reformation churches.

entries.title: The China Inland Mission founded
entries.blurb: At Brighton, James Hudson Taylor founds the China Inland Mission — interdenominational, inland-focused, its missionaries wearing Chinese dress — the pattern for a century of 'faith missions.'

entries.title: Irenaeus of Lyons
entries.blurb: Bishop in Gaul, taught by Polycarp who was taught by John — a living chain back to the apostles, and he knew it. Against the Gnostics he argued that the church's faith was public, handed down and the same everywhere, and he is the first writer we have who treats the four gospels as a settled four.

entries.title: Peter and Paul, Apostles
entries.blurb: Joint feast of the two great apostles, by tradition both martyred at Rome — Peter the apostle to the Jews, Paul to the Gentiles.

entries.title: The Westminster Assembly convenes
entries.blurb: The assembly of divines meets in Westminster Abbey to reform the English church; its Confession and catechisms remain the doctrinal standard of Presbyterian churches worldwide.

entries.title: Thomas the Apostle
entries.blurb: Feast of the apostle who doubted, then confessed the risen Christ as 'My Lord and my God,' and by tradition carried the gospel to India.

entries.title: Jan Hus burned at Constance
entries.blurb: The Czech reformer is burned at the Council of Constance despite a promised safe-conduct — a Protestant forerunner a century before Luther.

entries.title: Thomas More executed
entries.blurb: On the same date, 120 years after Hus, the Lord Chancellor Thomas More is beheaded for refusing to accept Henry VIII as head of the church in England — 'the king's good servant, but God's first.'

entries.title: Edwards preaches at Enfield
entries.blurb: At Enfield, Connecticut, Jonathan Edwards preaches 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' — the Great Awakening's most famous sermon, pleading with the unconverted to flee to Christ.

entries.title: The first Protestant mission to South Africa
entries.blurb: The Moravian Georg Schmidt lands at the Cape and begins work among the Khoikhoi at Baviaanskloof, later Genadendal ('vale of grace'). Expelled after seven years, his work outlived him: when missionaries returned fifty years on, his converts were still reading the Testament he left.

entries.title: Benedict of Nursia
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the father of Western monasticism, whose Rule — ordering a life of prayer and work, 'ora et labora' — shaped European Christianity for a millennium.

entries.title: The crusaders take Jerusalem
entries.blurb: After a five-week siege the armies of the First Crusade break into Jerusalem and massacre much of the city — Muslim, Jewish and Eastern Christian alike. Preached as a pilgrimage in arms, it left a wound between the faiths, and between the Latin West and the Christian East, that has never fully closed.

entries.title: The Great Schism (East–West)
entries.blurb: Legates of the pope and the patriarch of Constantinople exchange mutual excommunications, the symbolic break between the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.

entries.title: The Lausanne Congress opens
entries.blurb: On the anniversary of the Great Schism, the International Congress on World Evangelization opens at Lausanne — some 2,400 evangelicals from 150 nations; its Covenant, drafted under John Stott, weds evangelism and social responsibility.

entries.title: Vatican I defines papal infallibility
entries.blurb: The First Vatican Council promulgates Pastor Aeternus: the pope, teaching solemnly on faith and morals from his office, is preserved from error. Most Catholics received it; a body of German, Swiss and Dutch clergy and scholars could not, and left to form the Old Catholic churches.

entries.title: Mary Magdalene
entries.blurb: Feast of the first witness of the resurrection, called by the early church 'the apostle to the apostles.'

entries.title: James the Great, Apostle
entries.blurb: Feast of the son of Zebedee, one of the inner three, and the first apostle to be martyred.

entries.title: The Baptism of Kievan Rus
entries.blurb: Commemorated on the feast of Prince Vladimir: his people baptised in the Dnieper, turning the Rus toward Byzantine Christianity — the fountainhead of Russian and Ukrainian Orthodoxy.

entries.title: Mary, Martha and Lazarus of Bethany
entries.blurb: The household of Bethany whom Jesus loved — Martha who served, Mary who sat at his feet, and Lazarus whom he raised from the dead.

entries.title: The Transfiguration of Jesus
entries.blurb: On the mountain Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James and John, his face shining like the sun, with Moses and Elijah beside him and the Father's voice: 'This is my beloved Son.'

entries.title: Laurence, deacon and martyr
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the deacon of Rome who, ordered to hand over the church's treasure, presented the poor — and was martyred in the Valerian persecution.

entries.title: Dormition (Assumption) of Mary
entries.blurb: The oldest Marian feast, kept in the East as the Dormition ('falling asleep') and in the West as the Assumption — marking the end of the Virgin's earthly life. Not observed by most Protestant churches.

entries.title: Bernard of Clairvaux
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the abbot of Clairvaux, the dominant churchman of his century — mystic, preacher and hymn-writer ('Jesus, the very thought of thee') — whose Cistercians renewed European monasticism.

entries.title: Bartholomew the Apostle
entries.blurb: Feast of one of the Twelve, often identified with Nathanael, whom Jesus called 'an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.'

entries.title: St Bartholomew's Day Massacre
entries.blurb: A wave of mob and state violence against French Protestants (Huguenots) begins in Paris and spreads across France — thousands killed. A grievous day the feast now shares.

entries.title: Augustine of Hippo
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the bishop of Hippo, the greatest theologian of the Latin church — Confessions, City of God, and the doctrine of grace against Pelagius. See the vault's Augustine of Hippo note.

entries.title: The Slavery Abolition Act receives royal assent
entries.blurb: Slavery is abolished across most of the British Empire — a month after William Wilberforce died, having lived just long enough to hear the bill would pass.

entries.title: The Beheading of John the Baptist
entries.blurb: The church remembers the forerunner's martyrdom — beheaded by Herod for rebuking his marriage, at the demand of Herodias' daughter.

entries.title: John Bunyan
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the tinker-preacher of Bedford, imprisoned twelve years for unlicensed preaching, whose Pilgrim's Progress became the most-read book in English after the Bible. He died on 31 August 1688; the Church of England keeps his day on the 30th.

entries.title: Cluny Abbey founded
entries.blurb: Duke William of Aquitaine signs the charter founding the abbey of Cluny — free of lay control, answerable to Rome alone — the springboard of the great medieval reform of the church. The charter is dated 11 September; the year is given as 909 or 910.

entries.title: John Chrysostom
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the 'golden-mouthed' preacher and archbishop of Constantinople, greatest of the Greek Fathers as an expositor of Scripture, exiled for his plain rebukes of the powerful.

entries.title: Holy Cross Day (Exaltation of the Cross)
entries.blurb: A day to glory in the cross of Christ, kept since the fourth-century dedication of the church built over Golgotha in Jerusalem.

entries.title: Matthew, Apostle and Evangelist
entries.blurb: Feast of the tax-collector called from his booth to follow Jesus, and the writer of the first Gospel.

entries.title: The Peace of Augsburg
entries.blurb: The empire ends thirty years of religious war by letting each prince settle the confession of his own territory — cuius regio, eius religio. It bought peace and cost conscience: subjects who dissented could emigrate, and no one but Lutherans and Catholics was covered at all. The unfinished business ran on into the Thirty Years' War.

entries.title: The Society of Jesus approved
entries.blurb: Paul III approves Ignatius of Loyola's small company of graduates as a religious order under a fourth vow of obedience to the pope. Mobile where monks were settled, and schoolmasters by instinct, the Jesuits became the sharp edge of the Catholic Reformation and its most far-flung missionaries — Xavier to India and Japan, Ricci to China.

entries.title: Michael and All Angels (Michaelmas)
entries.blurb: A celebration of the angels and of Michael the archangel, 'protector of God's people' in Daniel and Revelation.

entries.title: Jerome, translator of the Vulgate
entries.blurb: The most learned and least easy-going of the Latin fathers, who went to Bethlehem, learned Hebrew, and translated the Scriptures from the original tongues into the Latin the West would read for a thousand years. His insistence on the Hebrew canon over the wider Greek collection set up the argument with Augustine that the Reformation would reopen. See the vault's Jerome note.

entries.title: The Baptist Missionary Society founded
entries.blurb: At Kettering, twelve Particular Baptist ministers — William Carey among them — found a mission society with a collection of thirteen pounds, putting Carey's 'Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God' into practice and opening the modern missionary movement.

entries.title: Francis of Assisi
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the merchant's son who embraced poverty to follow Christ, founded the Franciscan order, and preached the gospel to rich, poor and creation alike.

entries.title: William Tyndale executed
entries.blurb: Strangled and burned at Vilvoorde near Brussels for the crime of putting the Bible into English from the Greek and Hebrew. His last recorded prayer was that God would open the king of England's eyes — and within four years an English Bible built largely on his own work was licensed for every parish church. Much of its wording is still in the ear of anyone who reads the King James Version. See the vault's Tyndale's New Testament note.

entries.title: Council of Chalcedon opens
entries.blurb: The fourth ecumenical council defines that Christ is one person in two natures, fully God and fully man — the touchstone of orthodox Christology.

entries.title: Second Vatican Council opens
entries.blurb: Pope John XXIII opens the twenty-first ecumenical council, whose reforms — vernacular liturgy, ecumenical outreach — reshaped the modern Roman Catholic Church.

entries.title: Latimer and Ridley martyred at Oxford
entries.blurb: Bishops Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley are burned under Mary I. Latimer's words to Ridley endured: a candle lit in England that would never be put out.

entries.title: Ignatius of Antioch
entries.blurb: Bishop of Antioch, taken under guard to Rome to die in the arena. On the road he wrote seven letters to the churches — begging them not to save him, urging them to hold to their bishops, and giving us the earliest surviving use of the phrase 'the catholic church'. He is the clearest window we have into the church one generation after the apostles.

entries.title: Luke the Evangelist
entries.blurb: Feast of 'the beloved physician,' companion of Paul and author of both the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.

entries.title: The Peace of Westphalia
entries.blurb: The treaties signed at Münster and Osnabrück end the Thirty Years' War, which had killed perhaps a third of the German population over religion and power. Augsburg's settlement is extended to the Reformed, and Europe's rulers effectively give up on reuniting Christendom by force. The wars of religion end — not in agreement, but in exhaustion.

entries.title: Simon and Jude, Apostles
entries.blurb: Joint feast of two of the Twelve — Simon the Zealot and Jude (Thaddaeus), traditionally paired in mission.

entries.title: Reformation Day — the Ninety-Five Theses
entries.blurb: By tradition Martin Luther posts his theses against the sale of indulgences on the Castle Church door in Wittenberg — the spark of the Protestant Reformation. See the vault's Protestant Reformation note.

entries.title: All Saints' Day
entries.blurb: A feast of the whole company of the redeemed — 'a great multitude that no one could number' — from every nation, tribe and tongue.

entries.title: All Souls' Day (Commemoration of the Faithful Departed)
entries.blurb: A day of remembrance and thanksgiving for all who have died in Christ.

entries.title: The Rustenburg Conference opens
entries.blurb: Nearly a hundred South African denominations — including churches that had defended apartheid and churches that had suffered under it — meet at Rustenburg as the country begins to change. The Dutch Reformed theologian Willie Jonker confessed his church's guilt from the floor and Desmond Tutu answered him; the conference's declaration bound the signatories to restitution, not words only.

entries.title: Martin of Tours
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the soldier who, converted, shared his cloak with a beggar and became bishop of Tours — one of the first non-martyrs the church honoured as a saint. His feast, Martinmas, long marked the start of winter.

entries.title: The Fourth Lateran Council opens
entries.blurb: On Martinmas the Fourth Lateran Council opens under Innocent III — the largest council the medieval West had seen, defining transubstantiation and requiring annual confession.

entries.title: The Mayflower Compact signed
entries.blurb: Aboard ship off Cape Cod, the Pilgrims covenant themselves into a 'civil body politic' — the congregational church covenant applied to civil order. Signed 11 November by the old calendar, 21 November by the new.

entries.title: C. S. Lewis
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the Oxford don, apologist and storyteller — Mere Christianity, the Chronicles of Narnia — who died this day in 1963, an hour before the world's eyes turned to Dallas. Kept in the American Episcopal calendar.

entries.title: Urban II preaches the First Crusade
entries.blurb: At Clermont, Urban II summons the knighthood of Europe to the aid of the Eastern churches and the recovery of Jerusalem — 'Deus vult.' The crusades that followed left a legacy the church still reckons with.

entries.title: Andrew the Apostle
entries.blurb: Feast of the first-called disciple, who brought his brother Simon Peter to Jesus; patron of Scotland.

entries.title: Nicholas of Myra
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the fourth-century bishop famed for secret generosity — the historical root of Father Christmas — and, by tradition, a defender of Nicene orthodoxy.

entries.title: Ambrose of Milan
entries.blurb: A provincial governor acclaimed bishop by the crowd while he was still unbaptized, who gave away his property and set about learning theology in public. He taught the West to sing hymns, faced down an emperor over a massacre and made him do penance, and his preaching is what finally broke Augustine's resistance.

entries.title: The Cottesloe Consultation opens
entries.blurb: Weeks after Sharpeville, the World Council of Churches convenes South African member churches at Cottesloe in Johannesburg. The delegates — Dutch Reformed among them — rejected the scriptural case for apartheid. Verwoerd applied pressure, the Afrikaans churches withdrew their assent, and Beyers Naudé's refusal to withdraw his cost him his pulpit.

entries.title: Luther burns the papal bull
entries.blurb: At Wittenberg's Elster Gate, Luther publicly burns the bull Exsurge Domine and volumes of canon law — a point of no return in the break with Rome.

entries.title: Council of Trent opens
entries.blurb: The Roman Catholic Church's answer to the Reformation begins its long series of sessions, defining doctrine and reforming abuses. See the vault's Council of Trent (1546) note.

entries.title: The Nativity of Jesus Christ (Christmas)
entries.blurb: The birth of the Saviour at Bethlehem — 'the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.' The central feast of the incarnation.

entries.title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
entries.blurb: On Christmas Day in St Peter's, Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor — binding church and empire in the arrangement that would define, and haunt, Western Christendom for a thousand years.

entries.title: Stephen, the First Martyr
entries.blurb: The day after Christmas the church remembers its first martyr, stoned while praying for his killers — 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them.'

entries.title: John, Apostle and Evangelist
entries.blurb: Feast of the beloved disciple, writer of the fourth Gospel, three letters, and the Revelation.

entries.title: The Holy Innocents
entries.blurb: The church remembers the children of Bethlehem killed by Herod in his attempt to destroy the newborn king — the first to die for Christ.

entries.title: Thomas Becket martyred at Canterbury
entries.blurb: The Archbishop of Canterbury is cut down in his own cathedral by knights of Henry II after a long struggle over the church's liberties — Europe's most famous medieval martyrdom.

entries.title: John Wyclif
entries.blurb: Commemoration of the Oxford 'Morning Star of the Reformation,' who taught the supreme authority of Scripture and inspired the first complete English Bible; he died this day in 1384.
